newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to press Chechnya over kidnappings.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to press Chechnya over kidnappings.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin plans to press Chechnya's leader over the fate of Russian journalists and other hostages held in the breakaway region, the Kremlin said on Friday.

Diplomats from three countries whose nationals are held in Chechnya stepped up pressure for their release by urging Moscow to ensure the issue was raised when Yeltsin met Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov.
Yeltsin, who discussed preparations for the meeting with Kremlin security official Ivan Rybkin, hopes to have talks with Maskhadov soon.

"The (questions they will discuss) will surely include the revival of the Chechen economy, federal financial support for the republic, the seizure of people in Chechnya," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.
"The president will naturally inquire about what Chechen law enforcement agencies are doing to free the journalists."
Russian and Chechen officials are due to meet on Saturday to arrange the Yeltsin/Maskhadov meeting, expected to take place within days.

Yeltsin has sought to tackle Russia's most pressing problems since returning on August 5 from a month-long vacation. Chechnya, which dogged his first presidential term which ended last year, is high on his list.

Talks on normalising relations are stalled over Chechnya's status, an issue left unresolved when Russia withdrew its troops a year ago after nearly 21 months of fighting over the North Caucasus region's independence drive.

Maskhadov, who commanded the guerrilla forces which humiliated Russia's troops, says Chechnya is already independent. The Kremlin has ruled out full independence but promised the region wide autonomy.
Yastrzhembsky said last week Russia was also concerned that documents signed under a peace deal with Chechnya were not being put into effect.
Relations have been further complicated by dozens of kidnaps in the last few months in Chechnya and nearby areas which highlighted the lawlessness in the region.
Several Russians have been abducted and two Britons, five French people, one Slovak, a Yugoslav and a German are among those still held in the North Caucasus.
Rybkin, the secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, had talks on Friday with the German, British and French charges d'affaires.

The diplomats asked him to "include the problem of kidnapping people in the North Caucasus and the Chechen republic in the agenda of the planned meeting" between Yeltsin and Maskhadov, the Security Council said in a statement.
Rybkin said the Chechen leadership had achieved little in combatting the kidnappers. Federal and regional organisations must join forces to solve the problem, he said.
A Chechen official heading a special team investigating the abductions said a group which kidnapped several Russian journalists had been found.
Magomed Magomadov told RIA news agency the kidnappers had told they would be stormed by an assault squad unless they released the journalists in the next two days.
